title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Girl Among the Mill Wheels: Maggie's First Rebellion

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked — a close, passionate reading of George Eliot's great novel of the English midlands, childhood, and catastrophe.
Each episode, we move through the novel passage by passage, with three remarkable readers who never quite agree — and are all the better for it.
Our first guest is Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive.
Oliver reads every novel as a performer first — he hears the rhythms, catches the comedy, and knows when silence does the work prose cannot.
Then there's Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, lifelong Tory, and a reader who believes a novel's greatness lives in its moral imagination, not its social programme.
Edmund will hold us to the text when we drift — and deliver the occasional withering aside with perfect courtesy.
And Dr Daniel Rosen — cultural historian and a reader who finds in every novel an anatomy of class power.
Daniel believes great novelists were more radical than they themselves knew — and he earns that claim with evidence every time.
We open today in the world of Dorlcote Mill — with Mr Tulliver, a man of considerable self-regard and considerably less substance than he imagines.
Oliver, you've been given the passages that reveal Eliot's satirical eye at its sharpest — where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with a man who is, in the most precise sense, living on borrowed money and borrowed opinion.
Mr Tulliver carries a two-thousand-pound mortgage on his freehold, and yet — and this is the genius of it — he has almost entirely forgotten the fact.
Eliot tells us why, and the explanation is so perfectly observed that it makes you wince in recognition.

"He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance."
The jokes are doing the financial planning, you see.
And they gave — Eliot is exquisite on this — they gave a pleasant flavour to his glass on a market-day.
That is a complete psychological portrait in one clause.
What strikes me is that Eliot is not merely satirising Tulliver — she is describing a universal condition of human self-knowledge.
"As we are all apt to believe what the world believes about us" — that is the sentence that anchors the passage.
The comedy is real, but so is the pathos.
We laugh at Tulliver for forgetting the mortgage — and then we have the uncomfortable sense that we might very well do the same.
That movement — from irony to identification — is the hallmark of the greatest fiction.
I take Edmund's point, but I don't want us to dissolve this into pure anthropology quite so quickly.
Eliot is doing something very specific about the mechanisms by which ideology — in this case, the ideology of rural respectability — reproduces itself.
The jokes aren't innocent social lubricant — they are the means by which a man with a dangerous mortgage is kept in comfortable ignorance.
And look at where that ride through the Basset lanes takes us — Eliot gives us an entire devastated rural economy in a paragraph.
"Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than half a curate, also poor."
Five uses of the word 'poor' in one sentence — that is not comic repetition, that is an indictment.
Daniel is absolutely right about the accumulation — and as a performer, that list is a gift.
But Eliot then does something that I find almost cinematically precise — she gives us Mr Dickison's pub.

"A large low room with a sanded floor; a cold scent of tobacco, modified by undetected beer-dregs; Mr Dickison leaning against the door-post with a melancholy pimpled face, looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night's guttered candle."
'Irrelevant to the daylight' — I mean, who else writes like that?
Dickison doesn't appear again — he's a cameo — and yet he is unforgettable.
I want to draw attention to the sister — Mrs Moss — because I think she is too easily overlooked in all this.
Eliot notes that Tulliver's sister had come into the world in what the narrator calls 'that superfluous way characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages.'
That is the voice of patriarchal common sense — reported with savage irony, but reported faithfully.
A woman's existence is, in Tulliver's mental accounting, a financial liability from birth.
And yet — Eliot plants that detail about Mrs Moss's faded face beside the baby's fat hand pressed against her cheek.
It's one of those moments where the novel's sympathy quietly overwhelms its comedy.
And this connects to the other passages Oliver is carrying — because Eliot keeps returning to the absurdities of commerce and pride.
Take Tulliver's letter to Mrs Glegg — this extraordinary act of financial self-destruction dressed up as dignity.
He tells her the five hundred pounds will be repaid within the month — and then delivers this:
"she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
He is drowning and he insists on drowning with his chin up.
And then there's Bob Jakin — the pedlar — who is in another register entirely, and I adore him unreservedly.
When Bob is trying to sell Mrs Glegg a piece of figured muslin, he employs a sales technique of pure genius — the deliberate insult.
He tells her:
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
He is, of course, making her desperate to have it.
Bob speaks in dialect but thinks in pure strategy — he's the cleverest person in most rooms he enters, and the novel knows it.
Bob Jakin is one of those figures great novelists produce almost by accident — he overflows the function assigned to him.
He arrives as a comic turn and ends as one of the novel's genuinely good men.
The comparison to Tom is instructive — Tom who acquires three hundred and twenty pounds by orthodox hard work and moral severity.
Tom says to his father, with that peculiar quality of restraint that is his signature:
"I have three hundred and twenty pounds in the bank."
Eight words — and yet the weight of filial devotion, of years of self-denial, presses down on every one of them.
Edmund reads Tom as devotion — I read him as a man who has internalised the creditor's logic so completely that he cannot imagine any other form of virtue.
The three hundred and twenty pounds is real — the humanity it has cost him is real too, and the novel does not let us forget it.

What links Tulliver, Bob, Tom, and Mrs Glegg is that money is never merely money in this novel — it is the medium through which every relationship, every affection, every act of dignity or humiliation is transacted.
And it's precisely that economy of feeling — money as the grammar of every human relation in this world — that makes what comes next so devastating.
Because in the next segment we turn to the catastrophe at the heart of the novel's first movement — Mr Tulliver's ruin, and what it costs the family he built his sense of substance upon.

segments.title: The Weight of Patrimony: Mr Tulliver's Catastrophe

utterances.text: We've been watching Maggie push against the boundaries that childhood and circumstance have built around her.
Now we need to look at what happens to the world she's pushing against — the catastrophe that will reshape everything.
The Tulliver ruin is one of the great slow-motion disasters in Victorian fiction.
George Eliot builds it with such careful comic irony — and then, just as you're smiling, she pulls the floor away.
There's a passage I keep returning to — about Mr Tulliver's absolute, furious determination not to borrow from any client of Wakem's.
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
That's Eliot at full stretch — the comedy and the tragedy arriving in the same breath.
He swears he won't — and then external fact, as she so perfectly puts it, simply proves stronger.
The Œdipus comparison is not merely a flourish.
Eliot is making a serious claim about what kind of story this is — a tragedy of character meeting circumstance, not a social tract.
Mr Tulliver is not ruined by capitalism, or by the legal profession in the abstract.
He is ruined by the particular shape of his own will — proud, combative, constitutionally incapable of retreat.
And Eliot shows us that will operating through something as intimate as a marriage.
She tells us that Mrs Tulliver's pleading was, and I find this quite perfect—
"comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
But note where Eliot places the moral weight — not on the feather, but on all the weight already accumulated.
Edmund, I won't quarrel with the Œdipus reading — but I think Eliot's irony has a sharper edge than that.
The 'external fact' that proves stronger than Tulliver's will is not fate in any cosmic sense.
It is the specific structure of provincial credit and legal power — the way Wakem's network simply saturates the available world.
And look at what Eliot actually gives us in the portrait of Wakem through Tulliver's eyes.
This is the voice of a man who sees the system clearly, even if he cannot name it:
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
Tulliver's rage is inarticulate, but it is not wrong.
Wakem really is at the centre of every legal reversal he has suffered.
'A hook-nosed glib fellow, as cool as a cucumber' — there's something almost Dickensian about the ferocity of that hatred.
And yet Eliot never lets Tulliver become simply ridiculous.
His hatred has a dignity to it — the dignity of a man who knows something true and cannot express it in any form the world will accept.
What breaks me, every time, is how completely this catastrophe then flows into the children.
Tom seizes the burden of his father's debts and his father's hatred of Wakem — and he becomes their instrument.
That is the novel's most searching insight, I think.
Tom's exertion is genuinely heroic — and yet it becomes a weapon turned against his sister.
He says to Maggie — and this is delivered with the full weight of a man who has sacrificed everything—

"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both."
He is not wrong about his sacrifice.
And he is not wrong about the damage Maggie risks.
What Eliot makes us feel is the terrible pressure of being right about the wrong things.
Edmund identifies the cruelty of it beautifully — and I'd only add that 'respectability' is doing enormous ideological work in that speech.
Tom has internalised the Dodson standard — the standard of property, reputation, and visible standing — as the measure of his entire moral life.
Maggie's understanding of obligation runs deeper than that — and far more painfully.
She articulates it herself, later, with extraordinary precision:
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves.
They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
Tom's respectability is a social performance.
Maggie's faithfulness is a moral absolute — and it destroys her precisely because the world cannot accommodate it.
Tulliver's ruin, Tom's severity, Maggie's conscience — all of it draws the family into an ever tighter knot of obligation and recrimination.
And that knot, as we'll see in a moment, is most brutally visible in the relationship between a brother and a sister who once shared everything.

segments.title: Blood and Belonging: The Fracture Between Siblings

utterances.text: We've been tracing the collapse of Mr Tulliver's world — the mill, the debt, the ruin of a man who trusted his own will above all else.
But the damage doesn't fall on him alone — it radiates outward, and nowhere more sharply than between his two children.
Today we're looking at Tom and Maggie — siblings bound by love and separated by almost everything else.
What strikes me first — always — is how Eliot locates the fracture not in some great dramatic confrontation but in something embarrassingly small.
Tom pays attention to Lucy. That's it. That's all it takes.
And Eliot catches the exact moment Maggie's love curdles into something uglier — with this devastating little comparison.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse! There's the whole of Maggie in that image — this tenderness that can flip into something fierce the moment she feels displaced.
And what makes it so sharp is that she knows it. She's eight years old and she knows it about herself.
It is a moment of very precise moral observation, and I think we should resist the temptation to sentimentalise it.
Eliot is not apologising for Maggie. She is showing us the roots of a character who will, throughout the novel, struggle to govern her own will.
The child who wants to pinch Lucy in order to vex Tom is the same being who, much later, will make choices that devastate the people she loves most.
Eliot is a novelist of character — which is to say, she is a novelist of consequence.
I want to hold onto what Oliver said about smallness — because there's something structurally important in the way this jealousy operates.
Maggie's problem isn't just that she loves Tom. It's that Tom's approval is effectively the only currency available to her.
She has no independent standing in this family, in this society. Her value is entirely relational — she matters because someone who matters notices her.
When Tom turns to Lucy, Maggie doesn't just lose affection — she loses her only social position. That's not melodrama. That's the material condition of a clever girl in the 1830s.
And so she runs. Which is the other great thing Eliot does in these chapters — she takes Maggie's despair completely seriously while making it completely comic.
The resolution to go to the gypsies — listen to how Eliot frames it.
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That exclamation mark! "No!" — the sheer theatrical indignation of it. Eliot is inside an eight-year-old's head and she has the timing of a great comedian.
And then the gypsies would receive her "with much respect on account of her superior knowledge." The grandiosity is heartbreaking and hilarious in equal measure.
The comedy is inseparable from the pathos here — and what underpins both is Eliot's account of Maggie's education, or rather its alarming gaps.
The narrator's aside on Maggie's mind is one of the finest in the novel.
"In travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
"Small mind" is not condescension — it is a statement about the circumstances that have kept it small.
She knows "polygamy" and has deduced the meaning of "poly" by herself. She does not know that gypsies might be short of groceries.
That is not a stupid child. That is a brilliant child with almost no reliable information about the actual world.
And the fantasy collapses in a way that is both very funny and genuinely dark.
Eliot tracks the exact speed of Maggie's paranoia. From honoured guest to potential ingredient — in five minutes.
The passage is worth quoting in full, because the gothic precision of it is extraordinary.
"She had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking." Not just cooking — gradual. The child's mind generating the most precise horror it can manage.
But notice what Eliot says immediately after: Maggie's chief fear is not death but giving offence. She doesn't want the gypsies to think badly of her.
That is the social terror of the novel in miniature — the self-policing that begins in childhood and never really stops.
Now — and I think this is where the sibling bond becomes genuinely moving rather than simply comic — we have to reckon with Tom's side of it.
Tom away at school, grinding through Latin he cannot make sense of, is quietly lost without Maggie.
He had been brighter with her there. She'd been asking Stelling questions about the Roman Empire — questions Tom hadn't thought to ask.
And Eliot gives us this gorgeous, slightly absurd formulation of what Tom had actually learned.

"He had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
"A dim understanding." That is the most affectionate thing Eliot ever says about Tom Tulliver, and it costs him nothing and her everything.
Tom's suffering at school is, I think, consistently underread — and it matters enormously to understanding the later rift between them.
Eliot says something quietly devastating: under the pressure of Stelling's regime, Tom "became more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before."
His pride, which had always served him well, now meets only — as Eliot puts it — bruises and crushings.
And so he does something rather touching: he prays. Not from deep piety — but from sheer desperation.
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
There is no irony in that boy's voice. He means it absolutely. And Eliot lets us hear that — and smile — and ache at the same time.
The rigidity that hardens into cruelty in the adult Tom begins here, in a child trying desperately to be adequate to a world that was never designed for him.
Edmund is right that we should not reduce Tom to a villain — but I want to push on where that rigidity comes from.
Stelling's school is not a neutral institution. It is a machine for producing a certain kind of man — and it breaks the boys who don't fit the mould.
Tom is humiliated into a posture of hardness. He learns that the world rewards a particular kind of knowing and punishes everything else.
Then he comes home and applies the same logic to Maggie — her kind of knowing, her messy, dictionary-derived, question-asking intelligence, doesn't count.
The school didn't give Tom the tools to value his sister. It gave him the tools to dismiss her. And that, I think, is the deeper tragedy of this sibling relationship.
Two children, each shaped by a system that fails them differently — one confined to narrow knowledge, the other taught to dismiss what lies outside it.
And that system doesn't stop at the schoolroom door — it extends outward through debt, class, and the grinding machinery of provincial life.
Which is exactly where we're heading next.

segments.title: Class, Debt, and Drowning: The Social Machine Grinds On

utterances.text: We've been tracing the fracture between Tom and Maggie — that fault line running through the Tulliver family itself.
But Eliot insists that fracture isn't only personal — it's held in place by everything surrounding the family: class, debt, the whole machinery of provincial respectability.
And the machinery is extraordinarily precise in this novel.
Eliot gives us the Dodsons not as comic grotesques — though they are comic — but as a functioning ideology.
Their entire system of values is a theology of property disguised as virtue.
The narrator puts it with devastating precision — let me read the passage on their religion.

"Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it — if heresy properly means choice — for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma."
That last phrase — "like asthma" — is not a throwaway joke.
It positions religious affiliation as a hereditary condition — involuntary, constitutional, beyond examination.
I grant the satirical force.
But I think Eliot's attitude toward the Dodsons is considerably more complex than a simple indictment.
The narrator concedes — quite explicitly — that the Dodson code had a core of soundness.
Honesty, industry, faithfulness to kindred — these are not contemptible virtues dressed up as vices.
What Eliot diagnoses is the rigidity, not the content — the failure of imagination, not the failure of character.
That is a moral judgement, not a political one.
What I love is that Eliot cannot resist making the Dodsons funny even while making them frightening.
The dried tulip petals falling out of the Bible — the pages falling open not at Scripture but at pressed flowers.
That is a comedian's image delivered with the serenity of a philosopher.
But then you turn the page and there is Mrs Tulliver with her linens — and all the comedy drains away.
She is describing cloth she spun with her own hands, woven on a pattern she chose herself.

"To think o' these cloths as I spun myself... and Job Haxey wove 'em, and brought the piece home on his back, as I remember standing at the door and seeing him come, before I ever thought o' marrying your father!"
There is a whole life in that sentence.
A woman remembering herself before the catastrophe of her marriage — before she was a Tulliver at all.
And those linens are about to be sold to pay a debt that is not her fault.
The law — Wakem as attorney, the creditors, the bankruptcy proceedings — descends on the family and strips it.
Mrs Tulliver's linen is not a sentimental detail — it is labour.
She spun it, she marked it in a stitch so particular they would have to cut the cloth to remove it — her labour is literally woven into the fabric.
And the law simply dissolves that claim.
I wouldn't dispute the pathos of that scene for a moment.
But what makes it moving is precisely that it is about identity — about what a woman built and meant to pass on.
She says, "You'll never have one of 'em, my boy — and I meant 'em for you."
The grief there is not about capitalism — it is about a mother's broken promise to her child.
Eliot earns our tears by making the human specific, not by illuminating an economic structure.
That tension between the personal and the structural runs right through Tom's relationships too — not just within the family, but with Philip Wakem.
Daniel, you wanted to take up the question of what the novel says about whether two people from different worlds can genuinely befriend each other.
The narrator makes the structural argument with extraordinary bleakness in the passage about Tom and Philip's temporary reconciliation during illness.
It's a moment of genuine warmth — Tom cares for Philip, Philip is grateful — and the narrator immediately tells us it cannot last.
The image Eliot uses is a metallurgical one — a welding metaphor — and it's quite cold in its implications.
"If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out."
Boys must be made of metal that will mix.
The composition is fixed before the friendship begins — and what fixes it is precisely class origin, family name, whose father ruined whose.
And old Mr Tulliver has already told Tom exactly how to feel about Philip — in that wonderful line about the colt.
He says — and this is the man's entire social philosophy in a folk proverb —
"Ay, ay, the gray colt may chance to kick like his black sire."
So even in the moment of saying be kind to the boy, the father poisons the well.
Tom doesn't have a chance to see Philip clearly — the lens was fitted before his eyes were fully open.
Yet Eliot is careful to show us that Tom's severity toward Philip is not purely inherited bigotry.
He believes himself to be acting from duty — protecting his family, honouring his father's memory.
The narrator is ruthless about the self-deception involved — but the self-deception is itself a moral phenomenon.

"Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them."
That is not a portrait of a villain — it is a portrait of a man who has never been required to doubt himself.
And that, I would argue, is a deeper indictment than any structural analysis could provide.
I don't think the two explanations are in competition.
The narrator tells us Tom felt "the impetus of his indignation diverted toward Philip" — as if the hostility were already in motion and simply redirected.
And Eliot names what drives it: "an old boyish repulsion and of mere personal pride and animosity."
That repulsion has a history — it has the Wakem name, the class injury, the father's ruin written into it.
Tom isn't an autonomous moral agent making free choices — he is the product of everything that has been done to his family.
Which makes him both culpable and pitiable — and that is Eliot's genius.
And Maggie is caught in all of it — crushed between Tom's certainty and her own impossible conscience.
The passage where she's fighting the temptation of Stephen Guest is almost unbearable to read aloud — because she is so perfectly honest about her own worst self.
Eliot gives her this image — and it is one of the greatest sentences in the book:
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
"The best organs of her soul" — I've read that sentence forty times and it still stops me.
Eliot is saying that conscience and sympathy are not ornaments — they are the limbs by which Maggie walks.
Betray them and you do not merely sin — you cripple yourself.
That is Eliot at the height of her moral imagination — and entirely consonant with what I was saying about character tested by circumstance.
Maggie does not ask to be freed from the social constraint — she asks for the strength to bear it.
"Ah, God! preserve me from inflicting — give me strength to bear it."
That is a prayer, not a protest.
And it is a prayer born of a situation that was never of her making.
The Dodson code, the Tulliver debt, the Wakem enmity — all of it lands on Maggie's conscience as though it were her personal moral failing.
She internalises the cost of a system that has no interest in her wellbeing whatsoever.
The tragedy is that she does it with such extraordinary integrity — she is not deceived, she is simply loyal to something that crushes her.
What's remarkable is that Eliot never quite lets the darkness go unrelieved — even in the middle of all this grinding weight, there is wit.
Coming up next, we look at where the comedy lives in this novel — and why resignation, in Eliot's hands, can be one of the funniest things in English fiction.

segments.title: The Wit of Resignation: Comedy in a Collapsing World

utterances.text: We've been tracing the machinery of class and debt — now I want to turn to something that runs alongside that machinery: the comedy.
Because George Eliot is genuinely, often wickedly funny — and that wit doesn't soften the tragedy so much as sharpen it.
Oliver, you've spent more time inside this novel's voice than perhaps anyone — where does the comedy live for you?
It lives in the narrator's relationship with the reader — that conspiratorial warmth, that wink across the page.
Eliot is simultaneously a moralist and a comedian of the highest order, and she knows those two things are not in conflict.
Take Mrs Tulliver — thirteen years of marriage and still at it, still running her head against the same wall.
The narrator gives us the image, and it is absolutely perfect.

"Some minds are wonderful for keeping their bloom in this way, as a patriarchal goldfish apparently retains to the last its youthful illusion that it can swim in a straight line beyond the encircling glass."
The patriarchal goldfish!
Eliot gets the comic noun exactly right — not just a goldfish, a patriarchal goldfish, which somehow makes it both funnier and more devastating.
The comedy is inseparable from the pathos, I think — and that is precisely where Eliot's moral imagination is most fully engaged.
Mrs Tulliver is not merely satirised — she is understood, and even loved in the act of being laughed at.
One thinks of Dr Johnson's remark that life is not long enough for us to be indifferent to the happiness of others.
Eliot's comedy is never indifferent — it always costs her something to laugh.
There's a structural point worth making here, though.
The comedy about Mrs Tulliver's futility is not innocent — it's a comedy about a woman who has no leverage whatsoever in her own household.
She cannot persuade her husband because she has no institutional power over him.
So the goldfish swimming endlessly in its bowl — that image captures something about the circumscribed world of women in this society, not merely one woman's psychology.
Daniel's right that the bowl is the point — and the comedy about St Ogg's later is where Eliot lets that restraint go and becomes positively vicious.
The passage about how St Ogg's would have received Maggie had she come back as Mrs Stephen Guest is one of the most savage things in the novel.
And it opens with a line that is both a joke and a knife.
"We judge others according to results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived at."
The "how else" is what makes it sing — that shrug of complicity, inviting you to agree before you've quite realised what you're agreeing to.
And then she ventriloquises the whole of St Ogg's gossip — that maize-coloured satinette, poor Miss Deane! — in one long, horrifying rush.
What strikes me about that passage is how far Eliot implicates the reader — we are not permitted to stand above St Ogg's and smile.
The ease with which that community would have accommodated Maggie's transgression, given the right social outcome, is a portrait of moral cowardice — not a peculiarity of provincial life.
It is universal — and that, I think, is precisely what makes it comedy rather than mere satire.
The comedy about St Ogg's is also a very precise account of how respectability functions as a class technology.
It's not about morality at all — it's about whether your wealth and position are sufficient to convert transgression into mere indiscretion.
The post-marital trousseau redeems everything — not conscience, not character.
And the deformed young man, Philip Wakem, is discarded from the community's reckoning in a single clause — "he always was rather queer."
Before we leave the comedy entirely, I want to spend a moment with Tom in his disguise — because it is simply delightful.
Tom has dressed himself as a fierce warrior — burnt cork eyebrows meeting over his nose, red turban, red scarf, sword — the full effect.
But underneath the disguise are, as the narrator is careful to note, amiable blue-gray eyes and round pink cheeks that refused to look formidable.
"Philip had once told him of a man who had a horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a horseshoe on his forehead."
The frowning might — the earnest, futile, total commitment to making a horseshoe on one's forehead — that is a perfect small emblem of Tom Tulliver's whole character.
Wanting to be fiercer, grander, harder than nature made him — and the nature stubbornly, pinkly, refusing to cooperate.
The Tom passage connects, I think, to the much weightier passage about childhood suffering — the one Oliver hasn't yet quoted, but which I'd argue is the emotional heart of this comedy.
Eliot insists — rather polemically for a novelist — that the child's grief is real grief, not a rehearsal for the adult kind.

The passage that begins with Maggie among her shorn locks — sitting, the narrator says, "as helpless and despairing among her black locks as Ajax among the slaughtered sheep" — contains one of the great defences of childhood in our literature.

"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships; but it was not less bitter to Maggie—perhaps it was even more bitter—than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
"The real troubles of mature life" — held in inverted commas, as it were, by the word antithetically — that is a philosopher's move dressed as a novelist's prose.
And the Ajax comparison earns that philosophical passage — because Eliot has already made us laugh, and then she lands the Ajax image and the laughter catches in your throat.
The comedy and the tragedy arrive in the same breath — that is the technique.
What the passage also does — and this matters — is refuse consolation.
The adult world's standard reassurance — "you'll have real troubles soon enough" — is exposed as a kind of cruelty dressed as wisdom.
And in the context of Maggie's life, of course, the bitter irony is that the adults are correct — the real troubles are coming.
But that doesn't make the childhood suffering any less real — Eliot insists on that absolutely.
The childhood grief, the comic disguise, the savage ventriloquism of St Ogg's — they all converge on the question of what Maggie is being made into by all of this suffering.
Which is exactly where we're headed next — the hunger that shapes Maggie's character, and whether that hunger is a gift or a wound.

segments.title: Character Forged in Sorrow: Maggie's Hunger Transforms

utterances.text: We've been watching Eliot deploy comedy as a kind of pressure valve — the absurdity that survives when the world collapses around it.
But underneath all that wit, something else is being forged — Maggie Tulliver herself, shaped blow by blow through sorrow, hunger, and longing.
Edmund, you've been sitting with the passages that track Maggie's inner life from childhood onward — where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with a moment that Eliot herself calls a tragedy — and then immediately refuses to let be one.
It concerns small Maggie, consumed by her passions, and the fate of poor Lucy Deane.
Eliot gives us this extraordinary sentence — and I'd ask you to hear it carefully.

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action."
She is invoking Aristotle's concept of magnitude — the scale of event required to make catastrophe genuine.
The passion is real and enormous; the deed is — a child pushing another child into the mud.
That gap — between the intensity of Maggie's inner life and the smallness of what she can actually do — is where the whole novel lives.
And notice what Eliot does with Lucy in that same sentence — "poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud."
That is comic genius operating at full throttle.
The bathos — the Aristotelian invocation landing in a cow pasture — is absolutely deliberate, absolutely timed.
Eliot is laughing at Maggie, but she is also — and this is the difficult thing — entirely on Maggie's side.
What strikes me is the social dimension of that gap Edmund describes.
Maggie's inner life is outsized precisely because she has no legitimate outlet for it.
Later, when the family's ruin is complete, Eliot gives us a passage about young despair that I think is one of the most politically clear-eyed things in the novel.
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
"Though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present."
That rebuke — "we who looked on" — is directed squarely at the comfortable reader.
Maggie's suffering is not romantic adolescence; it is the structural consequence of poverty and confinement.
I take the social point, though I'd resist reducing it to structure alone.
Eliot's Maggie wants love — not justice, not opportunity — love.
The passage Daniel quoted makes it plain: "if life had no love in it, what else was there for Maggie?"
Nothing but poverty and her mother's narrow griefs — that is what waits for her without love.
The need is not a political grievance — it is a hunger that is older and more primary than politics.
And the place where that hunger becomes something close to unbearable is when Mr Tulliver is broken.
Eliot says it was "very early for her to know one of those supreme moments in life" — and she means it as something quite devastating.

"All we have hoped or delighted in, all we can dread or endure, falls away from our regard as insignificant; is lost, like a trivial memory, in that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
When I read that aloud — and I have read it aloud many times — the phrase "primitive love" stops me cold every time.
Not sentimental love — primitive.
That primitiveness is tested hardest, I think, in Tom.
Because in the scene of their shared grief — when Maggie's sobs finally break — Tom cannot weep.
Eliot writes it with a kind of spare Gothic force.
"He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank,—as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path."
The arm tightening convulsively — that physical reflex of love — and the blank, rigid face above it.
It is a portrait of a character in whom love has been shut inside a cage of will.
And Eliot does not let Tom off the hook, even as she explains him.
The passage on Tom's mind and prejudice is as clear-eyed as anything in the novel — and very nearly pitiless.
She writes, of minds like Tom's:

"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas."
"Something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton."
A staff to lean on, and a baton to beat others with — the ambiguity of that final image is precisely what makes Eliot a moralist rather than merely a critic.
She understands Tom from within even as she condemns what he does to Maggie.
And there is Mr Tulliver himself — old and broken and irreducible.
Maggie tells him she loves him, and he says — just this:
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
Eight words of dialect, and it is Lear on the heath.
That is what Eliot can do when she trusts the plainness of the thing.
Passion without the scale for tragedy, grief that cannot weep, love that cannot be returned — all of it flowing, inevitably, toward one destination.
In our next segment, we'll look at the force that shapes all of this — the river, the mill, the current that Eliot sets running from the novel's very first page.

segments.title: The Inevitable Current: Fate, Choice, and the Mill's Waters

utterances.text: We've been tracing how suffering shapes Maggie — how deprivation and longing forge something extraordinary in her.
But this novel is also, from its very first pages, a meditation on fate — on what the river carries and what it finally takes.
I want to close today by thinking about that current — destiny, memory, and what the characters can and cannot choose.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is that extraordinary opening gambit — the narrator waking from a dream.
Eliot gives us the whole world of Dorlcote Mill — the river, the machinery, the child on the bank — and then pulls the rug out.
She says, quite simply and magnificently:

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
The whole novel is already contained in that gesture — memory, loss, the past that is more vivid than the present.
And as a performer, I find that move thrillingly audacious — Eliot dares you to grieve for something she's already admitted is only a dream.
What Oliver describes is, I think, the deepest formal truth of the novel.
The entire narrative is structured as an act of memory — and memory, for Eliot, is not mere sentiment.
It is the very soil in which identity takes root.
There is a passage in which Eliot describes the childhood home with a precision that I find — still — almost unbearably true.

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
"The labour of choice" — that phrase is everything.
We do not choose our first loves — our home, our family, the mill itself — and that unchosen quality is precisely what makes them unconditional.
Maggie's tragedy is that she is too conscious, too awake — she feels the pull of memory and yet cannot stop herself straining against it.
Edmund's reading is genuinely moving, and I don't want to diminish it — but I think we have to ask what those childhood attachments are attached to.
The mill is not simply a symbol of innocent pastoral memory — it is a piece of productive property, contested, mortgaged, lost.
And the fates of the children — Maggie's vulnerability, Tom's burden — are directly produced by that economic catastrophe.
There is one moment where Eliot makes this devastatingly clear — Mr Tulliver riding away, then stopping, overcome by a single thought about Maggie.
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
That cry — "nobody but Tom" — tells us everything about what a world without property leaves a daughter.
Her fate is not cosmic — it is entirely legible as the fate of a woman in a society where inheritance, law, and custom conspire to leave her dependent.
The river doesn't take Maggie because fate is poetic — it takes her because every other door has been closed.
Daniel, that's fierce — and I think largely right — but I want to hold onto the formal power of that current as well.
Because the novel opens in a dream of the river, and ends in the river — and Eliot has engineered that from the very first sentence.
The water is doing double duty — it carries the weight of memory and the weight of structural inevitability at once.
And what I find most remarkable, as someone who has read this aloud more times than I can count, is that the ending still devastates.
The reader — like the narrator waking from the dream — knows it was always going to happen, and grieves anyway.
I think Oliver has named something essential — the inevitability that the novel cultivates is not fatalism but something closer to tragic recognition.
Eliot is very much an heir of the Greeks in this respect — and of Shakespeare.
What distinguishes tragedy from mere misfortune is that we sense the character could not have been otherwise — that Maggie's very gifts are what destroy her.
Eliot tells us that our affections have "a trick of twining round those old inferior things" — and Maggie's affection for Tom, for home, for the life she was born into, is precisely that.
She cannot sever the root without severing herself.
And yet — I keep returning to Tulliver on that horse, turning back, unable to go forward.
Eliot writes that he appeared "smitten by some sudden thought" — and the novel is full of these moments where characters feel the weight of what they cannot change.
For me, what the river figures is not simply poetic fate — it figures the accumulated force of social conditions that no individual will can resist.
Tulliver turns back not because he has given up on the future, but because he understands — in that inarticulate, body-level way — that his daughter has no future to turn to.
That is Eliot at her most radical — the tragedy is not in the stars, it is in the land registry.
The land registry — I love that.
Though I'd add: Eliot makes sure the land registry breaks your heart.
That's the genius — the social machinery is also always a human story, a family story, felt in the body.
"Poor little wench" — three words, and you feel the whole novel in your chest.
I think that is, in many ways, the perfect note on which to end — the human and the structural, the poetic and the political, held together by three words and a river.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, whose ear for the living voice of this prose never fails to illuminate what no annotation can reach.
To Sir Edmund Leigh, who reminds us that tragedy requires moral seriousness, and that Eliot was equal to that demand on every page.
And to Dr. Daniel Rosen, whose unflinching attention to power and structure reveals a George Eliot more radical, and more honest, than easy sentiment would allow.
Today we have followed the river from that dreaming narrator on the bridge all the way to the current that runs beneath every choice in this novel — and beneath every life.
To our listeners: thank you for spending this time with The Mill on the Floss.
It is a novel that rewards every return — and I hope today has given you one more reason to go back to it.

c8:p6.text:
For Mr Tulliver was in a position neither new nor striking, but, like other
everyday things, sure to have a cumulative effect that will be felt in the
long run: he was held to be a much more substantial man than he really was. And
as we are all apt to believe what the world believes about us, it was his habit
to think of failure and ruin with the same sort of remote pity with which a
spare, long-necked man hears that his plethoric short-necked neighbour is
stricken with apoplexy. He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about
his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of
land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of
considerable substance. They gave a pleasant flavour to his glass on a
market-day, and if it had not been for the recurrence of half-yearly payments,
Mr Tulliver would really have forgotten that there was a mortgage of two
thousand pounds on his very desirable freehold. That was not altogether his own
fault, since one of the thousand pounds was his sister’s fortune, which
he had to pay on her marriage; and a man who has neighbours that  will  go
to law with him is not likely to pay off his mortgages, especially if he enjoys
the good opinion of acquaintances who want to borrow a hundred pounds on
security too lofty to be represented by parchment. Our friend Mr Tulliver had
a good-natured fibre in him, and did not like to give harsh refusals even to
his sister, who had not only come in to the world in that superfluous way
characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages, but had quite
thrown herself away in marriage, and had crowned her mistakes by having an
eighth baby. On this point Mr Tulliver was conscious of being a little weak;
but he apologised to himself by saying that poor Gritty had been a good-looking
wench before she married Moss; he would sometimes say this even with a slight
tremulousness in his voice. But this morning he was in a mood more becoming a
man of business, and in the course of his ride along the Basset lanes, with
their deep ruts,—lying so far away from a market-town that the labour of
drawing produce and manure was enough to take away the best part of the profits
on such poor land as that parish was made of,—he got up a due amount of
irritation against Moss as a man without capital, who, if murrain and blight
were abroad, was sure to have his share of them, and who, the more you tried to
help him out of the mud, would sink the further in. It would do him good rather
than harm, now, if he were obliged to raise this three hundred pounds; it would
make him look about him better, and not act so foolishly about his wool this
year as he did the last; in fact, Mr Tulliver had been too easy with his
brother-in-law, and because he had let the interest run on for two years, Moss
was likely enough to think that he should never be troubled about the
principal. But Mr Tulliver was determined not to encourage such shuffling
people any longer; and a ride along the Basset lanes was not likely to enervate
a man’s resolution by softening his temper. The deep-trodden hoof-marks,
made in the muddiest days of winter, gave him a shake now and then which
suggested a rash but stimulating snarl at the father of lawyers, who, whether
by means of his hoof or otherwise, had doubtless something to do with this
state of the roads; and the abundance of foul land and neglected fences that
met his eye, though they made no part of his brother Moss’s farm,
strongly contributed to his dissatisfaction with that unlucky agriculturist. If
this wasn’t Moss’s fallow, it might have been; Basset was all
alike; it was a beggarly parish, in Mr Tulliver’s opinion, and his
opinion was certainly not groundless. Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a
poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than
half a curate, also poor. If any one strongly impressed with the power of the
human mind to triumph over circumstances will contend that the parishioners of
Basset might nevertheless have been a very superior class of people, I have
nothing to urge against that abstract proposition; I only know that, in point
of fact, the Basset mind was in strict keeping with its circumstances. The
muddy lanes, green or clayey, that seemed to the unaccustomed eye to lead
nowhere but into each other, did really lead, with patience, to a distant
high-road; but there were many feet in Basset which they led more frequently to
a centre of dissipation, spoken of formerly as the “Markis o’
Granby,” but among intimates as “Dickison’s.” A large
low room with a sanded floor; a cold scent of tobacco, modified by undetected
beer-dregs; Mr Dickison leaning against the door-post with a melancholy
pimpled face, looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night’s
guttered candle,—all this may not seem a very seductive form of
temptation; but the majority of men in Basset found it fatally alluring when
encountered on their road toward four o’clock on a wintry afternoon; and
if any wife in Basset wished to indicate that her husband was not a
pleasure-seeking man, she could hardly do it more emphatically than by saying
that he didn’t spend a shilling at Dickison’s from one Whitsuntide
to another. Mrs Moss had said so of  her  husband more than once, when
her brother was in a mood to find fault with him, as he certainly was to-day.
And nothing could be less pacifying to Mr Tulliver than the behaviour of the
farmyard gate, which he no sooner attempted to push open with his riding-stick
than it acted as gates without the upper hinge are known to do, to the peril of
shins, whether equine or human. He was about to get down and lead his horse
through the damp dirt of the hollow farmyard, shadowed drearily by the large
half-timbered buildings, up to the long line of tumble-down dwelling-houses
standing on a raised causeway; but the timely appearance of a cowboy saved him
that frustration of a plan he had determined on,—namely, not to get down
from his horse during this visit. If a man means to be hard, let him keep in
his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes, and
with the command of a distant horizon. Mrs Moss heard the sound of the
horse’s feet, and, when her brother rode up, was already outside the
kitchen door, with a half-weary smile on her face, and a black-eyed baby in her
arms. Mrs Moss’s face bore a faded resemblance to her brother’s;
baby’s little fat hand, pressed against her cheek, seemed to show more
strikingly that the cheek was faded.
c8:p6.summary: The narrator exposes Mr Tulliver's false sense of security despite carrying a two-thousand-pound mortgage, his unconscious blindness to his sister's suffering, and his weakness in lending to Moss; the passage then provides a scathing sociological portrait of Basset parish, its poor soil, poverty, and the temptations of Dickison's public house.
c8:p6.best_quote: He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance.

c13:p5.text:
Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I
leave you to judge what effect was produced on her by the reception of a short
letter from Mr Tulliver that very evening, after Mrs Pullet’s
departure, informing her that she needn’t trouble her mind about her five
hundred pounds, for it should be paid back to her in the course of the next
month at farthest, together with the interest due thereon until the time of
payment. And furthermore, that Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to
Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he
desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
c13:p5.summary: Mr Tulliver writes to Mrs Glegg announcing he will repay her five hundred pounds within a month and neither desires nor requires her favours, completely inverting her anticipated reconciliation.
c13:p5.best_quote: she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.

c34:p87.text:
“Eh, mum, I told you how it ’ud be,” said Bob, flinging aside
the coloured things with an air of desperation. “I knowed it ud’
turn again’ you to look at such paltry articles as I carry. Here’s
a piece o’ figured muslin now, what’s the use o’ you
lookin’ at it? You might as well look at poor folks’s victual, mum;
it ’ud on’y take away your appetite. There’s a yard i’
the middle on’t as the pattern’s all missed,—lors, why,
it’s a muslin as the Princess Victoree might ha’ wore; but,”
added Bob, flinging it behind him on to the turf, as if to save Mrs
Glegg’s eyes, “it’ll be bought up by the huckster’s
wife at Fibb’s End,—that’s where  it’ll 
go—ten shillin’ for the whole lot—ten yards, countin’
the damaged un—five-an’-twenty shillin’ ’ud ha’
been the price, not a penny less. But I’ll say no more, mum; it’s
nothing to you, a piece o’ muslin like that; you can afford to pay three
times the money for a thing as isn’t half so good. It’s nets
 you  talked on; well, I’ve got a piece as ’ull serve you to
make fun on——”
c34:p87.summary: Bob launches into an extended pitch for figured muslin as unsuitable for Mrs Glegg, comparing it to poor people's food, while emphasizing its former quality and current damage.
c34:p87.best_quote: You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite

c38:p23.text:
“A good while ago, my uncle Glegg lent me a little money to trade with,
and that has answered. I have three hundred and twenty pounds in the
bank.”
c38:p23.summary: Tom reveals that he borrowed money from uncle Glegg to trade with, which has grown into three hundred and twenty pounds in the bank, enough to pay the family debts.
c38:p23.best_quote: I have three hundred and twenty pounds in the bank

c13:p11.text:
Mr Tulliver’s prompt procedure entailed on him further promptitude in
finding the convenient person who was desirous of lending five hundred pounds
on bond. “It must be no client of Wakem’s,” he said to
himself; and yet at the end of a fortnight it turned out to the contrary; not
because Mr Tulliver’s will was feeble, but because external fact was
stronger. Wakem’s client was the only convenient person to be found. Mr
Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like
Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him.
c13:p11.summary: Mr Tulliver's search for a five hundred pound loan ends in ironic necessity: Wakem's client is the only available lender, presenting the narrator's philosophical reflection on Mr Tulliver as a man subject to tragic destiny.
c13:p11.best_quote: Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him.

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.
c15:p18.best_quote: it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back

c37:p53.text:
“Do what  I  require,” said Tom. “I can’t trust
you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you. Put your hand on this Bible, and
say, ‘I renounce all private speech and intercourse with Philip Wakem
from this time forth.’ Else you will bring shame on us all, and grief on
my father; and what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything
else for the sake of paying my father’s debts, if you are to bring
madness and vexation on him, just when he might be easy and hold up his head
once more?”
c37:p53.summary: Tom insists Maggie must put her hand on the Bible and speak the exact words of renunciation, claiming he cannot trust her, that she lacks consistency, and that while he has been working to pay their father's debts and restore family respectability, she has done everything to destroy both.
c37:p53.best_quote: I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both

c53:p29.text:
“That seems right—at first; but when I look further, I’m sure
it is  not  right. Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides
doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing
whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us,—whatever would
cause misery to those whom the course of our lives has made dependent on us. If
we—if I had been better, nobler, those claims would have been so strongly
present with me,—I should have felt them pressing on my heart so
continually, just as they do now in the moments when my conscience is
awake,—that the opposite feeling would never have grown in me, as it has
done; it would have been quenched at once, I should have prayed for help so
earnestly, I should have rushed away as we rush from hideous danger. I feel no
excuse for myself, none. I should never have failed toward Lucy and Philip as I
have done, if I had not been weak, selfish, and hard,—able to think of
their pain without a pain to myself that would have destroyed all temptation.
Oh, what is Lucy feeling now? She believed in me—she loved me—she
was so good to me. Think of her——”
c53:p29.summary: Maggie passionately explains that faithfulness means renouncing self-interest to honor the trust others have placed in us; she expresses anguish over her betrayal of Lucy and Philip, and argues she should have prayed harder to resist temptation.
c53:p29.best_quote: Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us.

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c14:p100.text:
But when this small apparatus of shallow quickness was fetched away in the gig
by Luke, and the study was once more quite lonely for Tom, he missed her
grievously. He had really been brighter, and had got through his lessons
better, since she had been there; and she had asked Mr Stelling so many
questions about the Roman Empire, and whether there really ever was a man who
said, in Latin, “I would not buy it for a farthing or a rotten
nut,” or whether that had only been turned into Latin, that Tom had
actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been
people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning
it through the medium of the Eton Grammar. This luminous idea was a great
addition to his historical acquirements during this half-year, which were
otherwise confined to an epitomised history of the Jews.
c14:p100.summary: Tom grieves Maggie's departure and credits her insightful questions about the Roman Empire with expanding his historical understanding beyond his textbooks.
c14:p100.best_quote: he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar

c14:p11.text:
Yet, strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl
than he had ever been in his life before. He had a large share of pride, which
had hitherto found itself very comfortable in the world, despising Old Goggles,
and reposing in the sense of unquestioned rights; but now this same pride met
with nothing but bruises and crushings. Tom was too clear-sighted not to be
aware that Mr Stelling’s standard of things was quite different, was
certainly something higher in the eyes of the world than that of the people he
had been living amongst, and that, brought in contact with it, he, Tom
Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid; he was by no means indifferent to this,
and his pride got into an uneasy condition which quite nullified his boyish
self-satisfaction, and gave him something of the girl’s susceptibility.
He was of a very firm, not to say obstinate, disposition, but there was no
brute-like rebellion and recklessness in his nature; the human sensibilities
predominated, and if it had occurred to him that he could enable himself to
show some quickness at his lessons, and so acquire Mr Stelling’s
approbation, by standing on one leg for an inconvenient length of time, or
rapping his head moderately against the wall, or any voluntary action of that
sort, he would certainly have tried it. But no; Tom had never heard that these
measures would brighten the understanding, or strengthen the verbal memory; and
he was not given to hypothesis and experiment. It did occur to him that he
could perhaps get some help by praying for it; but as the prayers he said every
evening were forms learned by heart, he rather shrank from the novelty and
irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic of petition for
which he was not aware of any precedent. But one day, when he had broken down,
for the fifth time, in the supines of the third conjugation, and Mr Stelling,
convinced that this must be carelessness, since it transcended the bounds of
possible stupidity, had lectured him very seriously, pointing out that if he
failed to seize the present golden opportunity of learning supines, he would
have to regret it when he became a man,—Tom, more miserable than usual,
determined to try his sole resource; and that evening, after his usual form of
prayer for his parents and “little sister” (he had begun to pray
for Maggie when she was a baby), and that he might be able always to keep
God’s commandments, he added, in the same low whisper, “and please
to make me always remember my Latin.” He paused a little to consider how
he should pray about Euclid—whether he should ask to see what it meant,
or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to
the case. But at last he added: “And make Mr Stelling say I
sha’n’t do Euclid any more. Amen.”
c14:p11.summary: Humiliated by repeated failures, Tom resorts to prayer, adding petitions for Latin and Euclid to his nightly prayers, showing his desperation and underlying sensitivity.
c14:p11.best_quote: and please to make me always remember my Latin

c30:p3.text:
Certainly the religious and moral ideas of the Dodsons and Tullivers were of
too specific a kind to be arrived at deductively, from the statement that they
were part of the Protestant population of Great Britain. Their theory of life
had its core of soundness, as all theories must have on which decent and
prosperous families have been reared and have flourished; but it had the very
slightest tincture of theology. If, in the maiden days of the Dodson sisters,
their Bibles opened more easily at some parts than others, it was because of
dried tulip-petals, which had been distributed quite impartially, without
preference for the historical, devotional, or doctrinal. Their religion was of
a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it,—if heresy
properly means choice,—for they didn’t know there was any other
religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like
asthma. How  should  they know? The vicar of their pleasant rural parish
was not a controversialist, but a good hand at whist, and one who had a joke
always ready for a blooming female parishioner. The religion of the Dodsons
consisted in revering whatever was customary and respectable; it was necessary
to be baptised, else one could not be buried in the church-yard, and to take
the sacrament before death, as a security against more dimly understood perils;
but it was of equal necessity to have the proper pall-bearers and well-cured
hams at one’s funeral, and to leave an unimpeachable will. A Dodson would
not be taxed with the omission of anything that was becoming, or that belonged
to that eternal fitness of things which was plainly indicated in the practice
of the most substantial parishioners, and in the family traditions,—such
as obedience to parents, faithfulness to kindred, industry, rigid honesty,
thrift, the thorough scouring of wooden and copper utensils, the hoarding of
coins likely to disappear from the currency, the production of first-rate
commodities for the market, and the general preference of whatever was
home-made. The Dodsons were a very proud race, and their pride lay in the utter
frustration of all desire to tax them with a breach of traditional duty or
propriety. A wholesome pride in many respects, since it identified honour with
perfect integrity, thoroughness of work, and faithfulness to admitted rules;
and society owes some worthy qualities in many of her members to mothers of the
Dodson class, who made their butter and their fromenty well, and would have
felt disgraced to make it otherwise. To be honest and poor was never a Dodson
motto, still less to seem rich though being poor; rather, the family badge was
to be honest and rich, and not only rich, but richer than was supposed. To live
respected, and have the proper bearers at your funeral, was an achievement of
the ends of existence that would be entirely nullified if, on the reading of
your will, you sank in the opinion of your fellow-men, either by turning out to
be poorer than they expected, or by leaving your money in a capricious manner,
without strict regard to degrees of kin. The right thing must always be done
toward kindred. The right thing was to correct them severely, if they were
other than a credit to the family, but still not to alienate from them the
smallest rightful share in the family shoebuckles and other property. A
conspicuous quality in the Dodson character was its genuineness; its vices and
virtues alike were phases of a proud honest egoism, which had a hearty dislike
to whatever made against its own credit and interest, and would be frankly hard
of speech to inconvenient “kin,” but would never forsake or ignore
them,—would not let them want bread, but only require them to eat it with
bitter herbs.
c30:p3.summary: The narrator details the Dodson and Tulliver code of life: a rigid, customary, semi-pagan Protestantism without genuine theology, focused entirely on respectability, proper funeral arrangements, ancestral duty, honesty, thrift, and the maintenance of family pride and property.
c30:p3.best_quote: Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it,—if heresy properly means choice,—for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma.

c22:p14.text:
“To think o’ these cloths as I spun myself,” she went on,
lifting things out and turning them over with an excitement all the more
strange and piteous because the stout blond woman was usually so
passive,—if she had been ruffled before, it was at the surface
merely,—“and Job Haxey wove ’em, and brought the piece home
on his back, as I remember standing at the door and seeing him come, before I
ever thought o’ marrying your father! And the pattern as I chose myself,
and bleached so beautiful, and I marked ’em so as nobody ever saw such
marking,—they must cut the cloth to get it out, for it’s a
particular stitch. And they’re all to be sold, and go into strange
people’s houses, and perhaps be cut with the knives, and wore out before
I’m dead. You’ll never have one of ’em, my boy,” she
said, looking up at Tom with her eyes full of tears, “and I meant
’em for you. I wanted you to have all o’ this pattern. Maggie could
have had the large check—it never shows so well when the dishes are on
it.”
c22:p14.summary: Mrs Tulliver describes in loving detail the linens she personally spun and marked, expressing her anguish that they will be sold to strangers and never reach her children.
c22:p14.best_quote: To think o' these cloths as I spun myself... and Job Haxey wove 'em, and brought the piece home on his back

c19:p38.text:
“Well, well,” said Mr Tulliver, “if he’s good to you,
try and make him amends, and be good to  him . He’s a poor crooked
creature, and takes after his dead mother. But don’t you be getting too
thick with him; he’s got his father’s blood in him too. Ay, ay, the
gray colt may chance to kick like his black sire.”
c19:p38.summary: The narrator reflects that despite the temporary reconciliation born of pity and gratitude during Tom's illness, the fundamental incompatibility of the boys' natures prevents lasting friendship; the warmth of shared suffering dissipates and they revert to their original suspicion and dislike, as metal of incompatible composition cannot permanently fuse.
c19:p38.best_quote: If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out.

c37:p64.text:
Not a word was spoken as they walked along. Maggie was suffering in
anticipation of what Philip was about to suffer, and dreading the galling words
that would fall on him from Tom’s lips; but she felt it was in vain to
